syllabus.clause: Cargo features are compile-time product variants and must be additive.

syllabus.clause: Feature unification across the dependency graph (resolver 2) and dev-dependency surprises.

at.step: Measured: consumer_b built alone genuinely prints "plain"; the identical consumer_b, built alongside consumer_a requesting fast_mode, genuinely prints "fast" instead, with its own source and Cargo.toml never touched

items.item: The non-additive and additive claims are measured by comparing one crate's own real stdout, built alone versus built in one cargo invocation together with a sibling that requests a feature on their shared dependency, rather than by inspecting Cargo.lock or a build log, so the claim is about the real, running binary's own behavior.

items.item: Each cargo build is preceded by deleting that workspace's own target directory, so an earlier invocation's own cached, unified result can never leak into a later, separately-invoked build and produce a false measurement.

at.step: Recap: a feature's own real combinatorics

items.item: The Cargo Book's features page and its dependency-resolution page are two genuinely separate pages describing two genuinely different real rules (unification, and the resolver's own historical default), giving this topic two sources rather than multiple quotes drawn from a single page.

at.step: The Cargo Book states these rules directly: cargo unifies the union of every feature requested on a shared dependency across the whole build, and a feature should stay additive so that enabling any combination of features stays safe. Do the three measured comparisons here model exactly the rule and the risk both quotes describe?

items.item: The specific names fast_mode, fancy, core_crate, consumer_a, and consumer_b are this specific example's own choice; the measured claims illustrate the real shape of feature unification and dev-dependency leakage for any real Cargo workspace at all, not a claim bound to exactly these names.

at.step: The identical comparison, but now consumer_a requests a genuinely additive feature, fancy, which only adds a new function and touches nothing consumer_b already calls. Does the output of consumer_b change this time?

items.item: An earlier draft of this topic's own third claim attempted to measure whether a prior --workspace build's own unified result would persist into a later, separate, non-unified build invocation; this was tested directly and found false (the later build genuinely reverts to the un-unified result), so the claim was redesigned around the real, reproducible dev-dependency/resolver contrast measured here instead.
